short: Trajan's two campaigns destroyed the Dacian kingdom and won Rome its richest new province.
full:
Dacia, north of the Danube under King Decebalus, had extracted humiliating subsidies from Domitian and remained a standing threat to the frontier. Trajan invaded in 101, defeating Decebalus at Tapae and imposing harsh terms in 102 that stripped Dacia of territory and fortifications. When Decebalus rearmed and violated the treaty, Trajan invaded again in 105, besieging and capturing the Dacian capital Sarmizegetusa Regia in 106; Decebalus killed himself to avoid capture.

Dacia was annexed as a new province, and its gold and silver mines financed Trajan's lavish building programme in Rome, commemorated on Trajan's Column. The wars marked the empire's territorial peak north of the Danube and brought waves of Roman colonists into the region, whose Latin-derived language survives in modern Romanian, the only Romance language east of Italy.
